\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{آتش} \ur{بازی} (ātish bāzī)}{آتش بازی (ātish bāzī)}]{\ur{آتش} \ur{بازی} (ātish bāzī) — fireworks}

\label{lesson:UR-C320-atish-bazi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to fly a kite, then the Urdu for to be cut.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{آتش} \ur{بازی}}
\textbf{\ur{آتش} \ur{بازی}} — \emph{ātish bāzī} — \textquotedblleft{}fireworks\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{رات} \ur{کو} \ur{آسمان} \ur{پر} \ur{آتش} \ur{بازی} \ur{ہوئی۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{rāt ko āsmān par ātish bāzī huī.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
There were fireworks in the sky at night.
\end{quote}

Feminine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{آتش} \ur{بازی}} (\emph{ātish bāzī}) is usually traced to Persian \emph{ātish-bāzī}, built from \emph{ātish}, \textquotedblleft{}fire\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{bāzī}, \textquotedblleft{}play\textquotedblright{}. It is feminine.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ātish bāzī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ātish bāzī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rāt ko āsmān par ātish bāzī huī.} — There were fireworks in the sky at night.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for to fly a kite, then the Urdu for to be cut, then say \emph{ātish bāzī} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ur{آتش} \ur{بازی} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Fireworks\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{پٹاخا} (paṭākhā)}{پٹاخا (paṭākhā)}]{\ur{پٹاخا} (paṭākhā) — a firecracker}

\label{lesson:UR-C320-patakha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to be cut, then the Urdu for fireworks.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{پٹاخا}}
\textbf{\ur{پٹاخا}} — \emph{paṭākhā} — \textquotedblleft{}a firecracker\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{بچوں} \ur{نے} \ur{گلی} \ur{میں} \ur{پٹاخے} \ur{چلائے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bachchoṅ ne galī meṅ paṭākhe chalāe.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The children set off firecrackers in the lane.
\end{quote}

Masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{پٹاخا}} (\emph{paṭākhā}) No dictionary we use records an older form, so its history is not settled; it is probably imitative of the crack it makes.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for to be cut, then the Urdu for fireworks, then say \emph{paṭākhā} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{چھڑکنا} (chhiṛaknā)}{چھڑکنا (chhiṛaknā)}]{\ur{چھڑکنا} (chhiṛaknā) — to sprinkle}

\label{lesson:UR-C320-chhirakna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for fireworks, then the Urdu for a firecracker.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{چھڑکنا}}
\textbf{\ur{چھڑکنا}} — \emph{chhiṛaknā} — \textquotedblleft{}to sprinkle\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{پھولوں} \ur{پر} \ur{پانی} \ur{چھڑکا۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{us ne phūloṅ par pānī chhiṛkā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
He sprinkled water on the flowers.
\end{quote}

Past, with \ur{نے} (he or she …): \ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{نمک} \ur{چھڑکا}, \emph{us ne namak chhiṛkā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{چھڑکنا}} (\emph{chhiṛaknā}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{chiṛaknā} under \emph{*chiṭ}, splash and scatter, a form it reconstructs (CDIAL 5035).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chhiṛaknā}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for fireworks, then the Urdu for a firecracker, then say \emph{chhiṛaknā} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{بھگونا} (bhigonā)}{بھگونا (bhigonā)}]{\ur{بھگونا} (bhigonā) — to drench; to soak}

\label{lesson:UR-C320-bhigona}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for a firecracker, then the Urdu for to sprinkle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{بھگونا}}
\textbf{\ur{بھگونا}} — \emph{bhigonā} — \textquotedblleft{}to drench; to soak\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{بارش} \ur{نے} \ur{سب} \ur{کو} \ur{بھگو} \ur{دیا۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bārish ne sab ko bhigo diyā.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The rain drenched everyone.
\end{quote}

Past, with \ur{نے} (he or she …): \ur{اس} \ur{نے} \ur{تولیہ} \ur{بھگویا}, \emph{us ne tauliyā bhigoyā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
is the causing partner of \textbf{\ur{بھیگنا}}, to get wet, which CDIAL lists for Hindi under a form it reconstructs (CDIAL 9500): you \textbf{\ur{بھگونا}}, and things \textbf{\ur{بھیگنا}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Urdu for a firecracker, then the Urdu for to sprinkle, then say \emph{bhigonā} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{جھومنا} (jhūmnā)}{جھومنا (jhūmnā)}]{\ur{جھومنا} (jhūmnā) — to sway (with joy or music)}

\label{lesson:UR-C320-jhumna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Urdu for to sprinkle, then the Urdu for to drench.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{جھومنا}}
\textbf{\ur{جھومنا}} — \emph{jhūmnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to sway (with joy or music)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ur{گانا} \ur{سن} \ur{کر} \ur{سب} \ur{جھوم} \ur{اٹھے۔}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{gānā sun kar sab jhūm uṭhe.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Hearing the song, everyone began to sway.
\end{quote}

Past (he …): \ur{وہ} \ur{جھوم} \ur{اٹھا}, \emph{voh jhūm uṭhā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{جھومنا}} (\emph{jhūmnā}) is inherited: CDIAL lists the Hindi cousin \emph{jhūmnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to shake\textquotedblright{}, under a form it reconstructs (CDIAL 3726); in Urdu it is swaying with music or joy.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling what happened.
\end{grammarlens}
